item.title: Should You Renew Your Tenant Before Winter Slows Leasing?
item.description: Renew or relist your Redding rental before winter? Weigh turnover costs, judge your tenant, set a fair renewal rent, and start the talk early.
item.content:encoded:
A good tenant who wants to stay is worth a careful look before you list, and October is the right time to have that conversation.

Winter Is a Bad Time to Find Out You Guessed Wrong on a Renewal.

October is decision month for a lot of Redding leases. If your tenant's lease ends sometime between November and January, the choice you make in the next few weeks will shape your winter.

 

Some owners renew without much thought. Others assume the lease simply ends and they can reset the rent or bring in someone new. In California , that is often not the case. More on that below. Trouble usually starts when the decision gets made late, or by default.

 

Here is how we help owners think it through.

 

Why Winter Changes the Math

Leasing has a rhythm. Summer is busy. Families move before school starts, and good listings get attention quickly. Once the holidays get close, fewer people tend to move. Weather turns, calendars fill up, and most renters would rather stay put until spring. That does not mean a home can't rent in December. It means you may have fewer people to choose from, and the wait can feel longer.

 

So the question is not only "What rent could this home get?" It is also "What would turnover cost me if it happens?"

 

What a Turnover Really Costs

We walked through the daily math in what an empty fall rental really costs Redding owners . Here is the short version. When a good tenant moves out, costs show up in a few places:

 

  • Vacant days. Every day between move-out and a new lease is rent you don't get back, plus utilities and yard care you now carry.
  • Make-ready. Cleaning, paint touch-ups, flooring, small repairs. Even a well-kept home needs some work between residents.
  • Marketing and showings. Photos, listings, answering inquiries, and meeting people at the property, often on evenings and weekends.
  • Risk. A new tenant is a new unknown. Good screening helps a lot, but you are trading a known track record for a fresh start.

 

None of that means you should never turn a rental. It means a small rent bump on paper can disappear quickly once the house sits empty.

 

Is Your Tenant Worth Keeping?

Not every tenant is a keeper. Most owners already have a gut feeling. It helps to check that feeling against a few plain questions.

 

  • Payment history. Do they pay on time, month after month, without chasing? An occasional late payment with good communication is different from a pattern.
  • Care of the home. What did the last inspection look like? Do they report small issues early, or do you find them later as bigger ones?
  • Communication. Do they answer when you reach out? Are they reasonable when a repair needs scheduling?
  • Lease compliance. Any complaints from neighbors, unapproved changes, or ongoing lease issues?

 

If the answers are mostly good, you have something valuable. A tenant who pays, cares for the home, and talks with you is hard to replace, especially heading into the slow season.

 

Base the call on how the lease has actually gone, and use the same standards for every tenant.

 

Setting a Fair Renewal Rent

Renewal is a natural time to look at rent. Start with what similar homes nearby are actually renting for, not the highest asking price you spotted online. Size, condition, location, and features all matter. If you want a second set of eyes, our free rental analysis is a good starting point.

 

Then check the rules. California's Tenant Protection Act (AB 1482) limits rent increases for many rentals to 5% plus the change in the cost of living, or 10%, whichever is lower, over any 12-month period. You can read the statute itself in California Civil Code section 1947.12 . Some properties are exempt, including certain single-family homes, but those exemptions come with conditions, including a specific written notice to the tenant. Don't assume yours qualifies.

 

Notice timing matters too. For month-to-month tenancies, California generally requires written notice at least 30 days before an increase of 10% or less, and at least 90 days before a larger one, under Civil Code section 827 . The California Attorney General's landlord-tenant overview explains both rules in plain language.

 

This is general information, not legal advice. Rules vary by property and situation, so talk with us before a notice goes out.

 

A fair renewal rent does two jobs. It keeps you close to market, and it gives a good tenant a reason to say yes. Pushing to the very top of the range can cost more than it earns if your tenant decides to start looking in November.

 

Start the Conversation Early

Timing is half the battle. We like to open renewal conversations well before the lease ends, early enough that both sides have room to think.

 

An early talk gives you:

 

  • Time to learn your tenant's plans before they start shopping
  • Room to meet notice periods without a rush
  • A head start on marketing if they are leaving, while more renters are still looking
  • A chance to fix the small things they have asked about, which goes a long way

 

Keep it simple and friendly. Thank them for taking care of the home. Put the proposed terms in writing. Invite questions. Our post on how to write a friendly rent increase letter has a few tone tips that still hold up.

 

When Relisting Still Makes Sense

One important note first. In California, many tenants who have lived in a home for 12 months or more are covered by just-cause rules. That means simply choosing not to renew a tenant who is doing everything right is generally not allowed unless the property is exempt. Some reasons for ending a tenancy also come with their own steps and requirements. No-fault reasons, such as an owner moving in, generally also require a relocation payment to the tenant. The Attorney General's overview above covers the basics. Every situation is different, so talk with us, and with an attorney where needed, before you decide not to renew.

 

With that in mind, relisting can make sense when:

 

  • Your tenant has already told you they are moving
  • There have been serious, documented lease problems, like unpaid rent or damage, handled through the proper notice steps
  • The home will be empty anyway and needs work

 

If you do relist heading into winter, go in with eyes open. Price it right from day one, get make-ready work lined up before move-out, and make showings easy to schedule, including evenings and weekends.

 

Wrap Up

A good tenant who wants to stay deserves a real look before you decide anything else. Weigh the cost of turnover. Look honestly at how the lease has gone. Set a fair rent within California's rules. Then start the conversation early.


﻿ Winter will come either way. Better to decide in October than to find out in January.

 

We handle lease renewals and turnovers for owners across Redding, Anderson, Shasta Lake, Cottonwood, and Shasta County. You can see how on our property management services page, or just give us a call. We are happy to talk it through, no pressure.

item.title: Fire Prevention Week: Smoke Detectors, CO Alarms, and Rental Fire Safety
item.description: Fire Prevention Week is a reminder for Redding rental owners and tenants to check alarms, practice safe charging, prepare for fire risks, and protect their homes.
item.content:encoded:
Small safety steps today can make a life-saving difference tomorrow.

Fire Prevention Week   is October 4-10, and this year's theme is " Charge into Fire Safety: Safe Charging Is a Superpower ," which focuses on everyday charging habits that reduce fire risk. Here in Redding, we know how quickly fire can change lives. If you own a rental in Shasta County, Anderson, Palo Cedro, or Lake California, or you rent a home in Cottonwood or Shasta Lake, fire safety is a shared responsibility .

This guide covers who is responsible for what, how often to test your alarms, and how to protect yourself financially.


What California law requires of owners

Working alarms are not optional in a rental. A few key points:

  • Alarms must work when a tenant moves in. When a new tenancy begins, the owner must ensure the smoke alarms are operable. public
  • Placement matters. Smoke alarms are generally required in each sleeping room, outside sleeping areas, and on every level of the home.
  • Carbon monoxide alarms are required too. California requires CO devices in existing dwellings, typically on each level and outside sleeping areas. They are required in homes with any fuel-burning appliance. ( California Health & Safety Code, Sections 13113.7 and 17926 )
  • Battery rules. Battery-only smoke alarms must use a sealed battery that lasts at least 10 years. Combination smoke/CO alarms are allowed and popular with owners because they simplify upkeep.
  • Owners must fix reported problems. The owner or agent must correct any reported deficiency, and is not in violation for a faulty alarm they weren't told about. That makes tenant reporting important. (Health and Safety Code section 13113.7 )

Owner tip: Document everything. Record the alarm locations, manufacture dates, and test results at move-in and at every inspection. If an incident ever occurs, a paper trail is your best protection.

What tenants are responsible for

  • Report problems right away. Tenants are responsible for notifying the owner or manager if they learn an alarm is inoperable. Do it in writing so there's a record. California Public Law Health and Safety Code section 13113.7
  • Never disable or tamper with alarms. Pulling a battery to stop a cooking chirp may feel harmless, but tampering with a smoke detector or fire protection device is a misdemeanor under California Penal Code Section 148.4 . More importantly, it removes the one thing that wakes you at 2 a.m.
  • Test regularly and keep the area clear. Keep dust, paint, and stored items off the alarm.

    SMOKE DETECTOR, CARBON MONOXIDE ALARM & FIRE EXTINGUISHER SELF-CERTIFICATION & INSPECTION FORM

Safe charging: this year's theme

Phones, laptops, e-bikes, scooters, and power tools all run on lithium-ion batteries. They are generally safe when used properly, but damaged batteries or improper charging can cause them to overheat and ignite.

Simple habits help:

  • Use the charger that came with the device, or one certified for it.
  • Charge on a hard surface, not on a bed, couch, or pile of clothes.
  • Don't charge e-bikes or scooters while you sleep, and don't block your exit with them.
  • Stop using any battery that swells, leaks, smells odd, or gets unusually hot.

For owners: Consider adding e-bike and scooter charging and storage guidelines to your lease. It's a growing issue, and a clear policy protects everyone.

Fall and winter fire risks in our area

As temperatures drop across Shasta County, heating season brings its own risks:

  • Space heaters: Plug them directly into the wall, never an extension cord, and keep them at least 3 feet from anything flammable.
  • Wood stoves and fireplaces: Have chimneys inspected and cleaned before the first fire, and check your lease for rules on their use.
  • Generators during outages: If power is shut off, run generators outdoors only, well away from windows and doors. Never run one in a garage. This is a leading cause of carbon monoxide poisoning.
  • Candles: Skip them as outage lighting. Use flashlights or battery lanterns.
  • Wildfire readiness: Keep gutters and roofs clear of pine needles and leaves, and review your evacuation plan.


Renters insurance: the safety net many tenants skip

A property owner's insurance generally covers the building, not a tenant's personal belongings. After a fire, a tenant without renters insurance may lose everything with no way to replace it.

A typical policy covers:

  • Personal belongings (furniture, clothing, electronics)
  • Temporary housing if the home becomes unlivable
  • Personal liability if the tenant accidentally causes damage

Policies are usually inexpensive for the protection they provide. For owners, requiring renters insurance in the lease reduces disputes and financial exposure after a loss.

A quick fire safety checklist

Tenants:

  • ☐ Test every alarm this week
  • ☐ Plan two exits from every room and a meeting spot outside
  • ☐ Check your chargers, cords, and e-bike storage
  • ☐ Confirm you have renters insurance

Owners:

  • ☐ Verify alarm placement and manufacture dates in every unit
  • ☐ Replace any alarm past its service life
  • ☐ Document inspections and tenant notices
  • ☐ Review your lease for charging, heater, and insurance language

How Authority Property Management helps

Keeping up with safety compliance, inspections, and documentation is exactly why many owners choose professional management . We handle alarm checks at move-in, respond quickly to repair requests, and keep records organized across our properties.

  • Owners and investors: Wondering what your property could earn with professional management? [ Get your free rental analysis here ]
  • Tenants: Looking for a well-maintained home? [ Browse available rentals ]
  • Questions about fire safety, leases, or management? [ Talk to our team ]

**This article is for general information and isn't legal advice. Requirements can vary by property type and local jurisdiction, so check with your local fire department or an attorney for your situation.

item.title: What an Empty Fall Rental Really Costs Redding Owners
item.description: A vacant Redding rental costs more than lost rent. See the daily math, a worked example, a free calculator, and ways to cut empty days this fall.
item.content:encoded:
Lost rent is only part of it. Utilities, yard care, and every extra week on the market add up faster than most owners expect.

An Empty House Still Bills You Every Day.

Summer is the busy season for rentals in Redding. Families move before school starts, leases roll over, and the phone rings. Then fall shows up. School is back in session, the holidays get closer, and fewer people are out looking for a new place to live.


If your rental is sitting empty right now, you are not alone, and you have not done anything wrong. But it helps to know what that empty house is actually costing you. Most owners think about the rent they are missing. Fewer add up the bills that continue while nobody lives there.


The Real Daily Cost of an Empty Rental

A vacant rental costs you in two ways.


Lost rent. Every day without a tenant is a day of rent you will not get back. To turn monthly rent into a daily number, multiply the monthly rent by 12 and divide by 365. That spreads a year of rent across every day of the year, so short and long months even out.


Carrying costs . When the tenant moves out, many bills shift back to you. Common ones include:

  • Electric and gas, so the lights work for showings and the house stays at a safe temperature
  • Water, sewer, and trash
  • Lawn care or landscaping, because a brown yard makes a bad first impression
  • Pest control
  • Pool service, if the property has one
  • Other fixed costs like HOA dues, insurance, or mortgage interest, which do not stop just because the house is empty


Add those together and run them through the same math (monthly rent × 12 ÷ 365). Lost rent per day plus carrying costs per day is what one empty day really costs you.


A Worked Example: Two Homes (Illustrative Numbers)

Here is how the math plays out on two homes. These are round, illustrative numbers for the example, not Redding averages, not sourced statistics, and not any specific property. Swap in your own.


Home 1: $1,800 a month. Lost rent is about $60 a day.


Home 2: $2,600 a month. Lost rent is about $87 a day.


(Those are quick estimates, monthly rent divided by 30. The more precise monthly rent × 12 ÷ 365 formula, which the calculator below uses, gives about $59 and $85.)


Then add the bills that continue while the house is empty:

  • Utilities: about $200 per month
  • Landscaping: about $150 to $175 per month
  • Mortgage and insurance payments, where applicable


Depending on the home, those outgoing costs add roughly $15 to $45 a day on top of the lost rent.


Total: roughly $75 to $130 for every day the house sits empty.


In plain terms, an empty rental like this can cost you $75 to well over $100 a day. At $75 a day, a 30-day vacancy costs about $2,250. At $130 a day, it costs about $3,900. And that is before cleaning, repairs, or a single dollar spent on marketing.


If you want a real Redding reference point for rent, HUD publishes Fair Market Rents for the Redding metro area . For fiscal year 2026, HUD's figure is $1,590 for a two-bedroom and $2,211 for a three-bedroom. Keep in mind those are HUD program benchmarks that include utilities, not a pricing tool for your specific house.


How to Cut Your Vacancy Days

You can't control the season. You can control a lot of what happens while the house is empty.


Price it right on day one. Overpricing feels safe, but it often costs more than it earns. Using the $1,800 home above at about $75 a day: pricing the home $50 lower per month costs $600 over a 12-month lease. If that lower price rents the home just two weeks sooner, it saves about $1,050 in empty days. If you are not sure where your rent should land, a free rental analysis is a good place to start.


Speed up the turnover. Every day between move-out and "ready to show" is a vacant day. Schedule the walk-through, cleaning, paint, and repairs before the tenant leaves, not after. Line up vendors early so the work happens back to back.


Market it like you mean it. Clear, bright photos. An honest, complete description. A listing that appears where renters are actively searching. Take a look at our current Redding rental listings to see how the homes we manage are presented.


Make showings easy. Answer inquiries fast. Offer times that work for people with jobs, including evenings and weekends. A renter who waits two days for a reply has often already found somewhere else.


Keep the good tenant you already have. The cheapest vacancy is the one that never happens. Start the renewal conversation well before the lease ends, fix the small things they have asked about, and treat a good tenant as a valuable part of your rental investment. Nationally, the U.S. Census Bureau put the rental vacancy rate at 7.3% in the second quarter of 2026 . That is a national number, not a Redding one, but it is a reminder that renters have choices, and a tenant who feels taken care of is more likely to stay.


Try the Vacancy Cost Calculator

Want to see your own numbers? Use the calculator below. Enter your monthly rent, the utilities you carry while the home is empty, your yard, pest, and pool services, and any other monthly costs. It shows your daily vacancy cost, a breakdown of expenses, and what a 7-day, 30-day, or 60-day vacancy could cost.

The result is an estimate. It does not include turnover repairs, cleaning, or taxes, so your true cost may be higher.


The Bottom Line

An empty rental is never free. Even a modest daily cost turns into real money over a few weeks, and fall is when those weeks can stretch. The owners who come out ahead are the ones who price with care, turn the house quickly, market it well, and hold on to good tenants.


If you would rather have someone else handle the pricing, marketing, showings, and renewals, take a look at our property management services and our published pricing . Or give us a call at 530-410-6085 . We are happy to talk through your numbers, no pressure.

﻿

At Authority Property Management , We Make Rentals Simple .

item.title: Should You Sell Your Redding Rental? Tax and Tenant Pitfalls to Weigh First
item.description: Think beyond the sale price. Protect your investment, your income, and your tenant relationship.
item.content:encoded:
Before anyone walks your occupied rental, understand depreciation recapture, capital gains, and what a “just looking” visit can do to a good tenant. ﻿

The Listing Appointment Is Not the First Step.

Selling a rental in Redding , Anderson , Shasta Lake , Cottonwood , or anywhere in Shasta County can be the right call. Liquidity matters. So does sleep.


The order of operations matters more than most owners think. The listing appointment is not the first step. A clear talk with your tax professional is.

This post is for owners who already have a house working for them and are weighing whether to cash out. It is general information, not tax or legal advice. Your facts, basis, depreciation history, filing status, and residency determine the actual tax outcome.


A Hypothetical Situation

In one situation we recall an owner was considering selling and wanted a soft look at the market. An agent walked the occupied house. The resident saw strangers with clipboards and, understandably, got concerned. Within weeks the resident gave notice and moved out.


Then the tax picture came into focus. After talking with their tax professional about depreciation recapture, capital gains , and what a sale would actually mean, the owner decided not to sell. The property was never listed. But the house was already empty. The owner had to find a new tenant, carry a vacancy with no rental income for a stretch, and cover the turn costs that come with any move-out. The sale never happened. The vacancy still did, and it was costly.


That is the pitfall this post is about for owners who are considering selling: looking before you have decided can cost you a good tenant and months of income, even when you ultimately choose to keep the property.


What the tax picture can include

When you sell a rental, the IRS does not start with your sale price. It starts with your adjusted basis .


Under IRS Publication 544 (2025 edition, for preparing 2025 returns), gain is generally amount realized minus adjusted basis. Depreciation you took, or that you could have taken, reduces that basis.  Publication 527 makes the same point for rental property: skipping a depreciation claim does not mean you get to keep a higher basis later.


Part of the gain on depreciated real estate can be unrecaptured section 1250 gain . Per IRS Topic 409 (reviewed/updated February 25, 2026), that layer is taxed at a federal maximum of 25%.


If you held the property more than one year, the rest of a long-term capital gain may fall into the preferential federal brackets Topic 409 describes for taxable years beginning in 2025: 0%, 15%, or 20% for most individuals, depending on taxable income. Short-term gains are taxed as ordinary income. Some owners may also face the 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax (NIIT) described in IRS Topic 559 (reviewed/updated April 2, 2026). Whether that applies depends on your income and how the gain is characterized. Do not assume it does or does not.


California is different. The  Franchise Tax Board is plain about it: California does not have a lower rate for capital gains . Gains are taxed as ordinary income. The 2025 California tax rate schedules list ordinary brackets up to 12.30%. Separately, the Behavioral Health Services Tax adds 1% on taxable income over $1,000,000 (2025 Form 540-ES instructions). If someone casually says “about 13.3%,” they are describing that top ordinary bracket plus the high-income layer, not a special California capital gains rate.


We have written before about how depreciation works while you own a rental . The sale is when that history shows up again.


An illustrative example (labeled hypothetical)

Here is a labeled hypothetical, not a prediction for your house.

Say an owner bought a rental years ago for $280,000, held it long enough for long-term treatment, and took $70,000 of building depreciation. Adjusted basis on the building side is now much lower than purchase price. They are looking at a sale around $420,000 before selling costs.


In that made-up file, part of the gain can sit in the federal unrecaptured section 1250 layer (up to the 25% maximum on Topic 409), with additional long-term capital gain possibly taxed at 0%, 15%, or 20% depending on their taxable income, plus possible NIIT if they are over the Topic 559 thresholds. California would generally tax the gain as ordinary income under the FTB rules above.


Those numbers are story props. Your purchase price, improvements, depreciation schedule, selling costs, filing status, and year of sale will change every line. A CPA, enrolled agent, or other qualified tax professional should run your actual worksheet before you set a list price.


A short note on 1031 exchanges

Some owners ask about a like-kind exchange under section 1031. At a high level, a properly structured exchange of real property held for investment or business use for other like-kind real property can defer recognition of gain rather than erase it. Personal-use property and property held primarily for sale generally do not qualify.


Deferred exchanges have strict identification and receipt timing (commonly discussed as 45 days to identify and 180 days to receive, or earlier if your return due date including extensions comes first). See Publication 544 and the Form 8824 instructions (2025).


California owners who exchange California property for out-of-state property may also have ongoing Franchise Tax Board reporting on Form 3840 until deferred California-source gain is recognized. This is not a do-it-yourself checklist. Talk with your tax professional and, if you proceed, a qualified intermediary.


What “just looking” feels like to a tenant

One more operational point, separate from the tax math.

A showing that feels casual to you can feel like a notice to the person living there. They hear footsteps, see a lockbox conversation, and start planning their next move. California notice and deposit rules still apply if they leave. You can end up with a vacant house even if you never list.


Better sequence for most current owners: tax conversation first, then a real hold-or-sell decision, then a plan that respects the lease and clear resident communication if you do proceed. We have also walked through rent-versus-sell framing for local owners when the question is bigger than one afternoon with an agent.


Wrap Up

You can sell. Plenty of owners should.

Just do it with eyes open. Depreciation history, federal layers, California ordinary-income treatment, and the risk of unsettling a good tenant are all part of the same decision. Speak with a tax professional before the first walkthrough. Then decide what the market should see.


If you want the house to stay calm while you think, keep the day-to-day quiet. The listing appointment can wait until the tax picture is clear.


At Authority Property Management, We Make Rentals Simple!

Call 530-410-6085 if you want to talk through the operational side of a hold-or-sell decision on a home we already manage.

Or visit our website at www.authoritypm.com for more info.


﻿

item.title: September 2026 Redding Rental Market Update for Property Owners
item.description: September’s Redding rental update covers occupancy, sales trends, AB 414 deposit reminders, fall maintenance, leasing strategy, and local community events.
item.content:encoded:
Fall leasing, Shasta County sales signals, and practical owner prep as Redding cools from summer heat.

September is a transition month in Redding . The heat eases, school routines settle, and summer vacancies get a fresh look from serious applicants.

This month: our portfolio occupancy snapshot, Shasta County sales (and what we are seeing when rentals try the for-sale route), a mid-year AB 414 deposit -refund reminder, fall maintenance, Anderson Chamber Greeters at our office, our Best of North State nominations , and a couple of local weekends still on the calendar.


Redding Rental Market Update

Across our managed portfolio as of September 14, occupancy sits at 92.8% (920 occupied of 991 active units). That leaves 71 vacant units: 11 already re-rented and awaiting move-in, and 60 still available, for about a 7.2% vacancy rate. Another 21 units are on notice (4 already re-rented, 17 still to fill), so fall make-ready and showing response stay important.


Those are our figures only. For owners, the basics still win: clean units, honest comps, fast showing response, and make-ready that photographs well. Watch days on market and showing feedback more than last year’s rent. If a home is sitting, review photos, price, and condition with our leasing team before fall slows further. If you want a second look at positioning, start with our property management pricing and management services pages.


Shasta County Sales Market Snapshot

Sales still matter for rental investors, even when you are not listing.


Per Josh Barker’s September 2026 Shasta County update on reddinghomes.com/blog (sales source), August closed 233 homes versus 228 a year earlier (+2.2%). Year to date, 1,791 sales versus 1,708 (+4.9%). Inventory is tighter: 946 active listings versus 1,059 last August (−10.7%), and 323 new listings versus 341 (−5.3%).

Median sale price hit $385,000 versus $357,000 (+7.8%); average was $436,772 (+4.8%). Absorption is about 4.32 months versus 5.26 a year ago (balanced, slight seller edge when priced right). Strongest band: roughly $250,000 to $500,000. Days on market improved (85 listing-to-close vs 95; median DOM 66 vs 75).


A 30-year fixed averaged around 7.125%, up from about 6.75% the prior month. Redding SFR permits through June 30 were 49 versus 135 (about −64%). Josh notes DR Horton is winding down remaining inventory; Palomar sells roughly 50 to 60 homes a year.

What we are seeing on our side: quite a few rental homes go up for sale, then sit with little or no activity for about two to four months. Owners bring them back to us to get rented.


We are watching the same properties leave the rental pool for a sale listing and come right back when the market does not cooperate.

﻿

Owner takeaway: Higher rates keep some households renting longer. Tight sales inventory supports values when a home is priced right, but a slow sale can cost months of vacancy. If a listing is quiet, a clean rental plan often beats waiting it out empty. Owners weighing that fork in the road may also find our recent piece on selling versus keeping a Redding rental useful.


Legislative Lowdown: AB 414 Electronic Deposit Refunds

California AB 414 took effect January 1, 2026, and updated how residential security deposits can be returned under Civil Code section 1950.5. Mid-year reminder, not a brand-new headline.


In plain English: if rent or the original security deposit was received electronically, the deposit return process may need an electronic refund path, with the tenant designating an account or method in writing. Owners and tenants can also agree in writing to another return method. Keep move-out checklists and written consent records tidy so timing expectations around the deposit and itemized statement stay on track.


This section is informational only. It is not legal advice. Owners should review this with their attorney or trusted professional when needed.


Seasonal Maintenance Tips

After peak Redding heat, a short fall pass protects the asset and cuts surprise calls:


  • Change HVAC filters and schedule service if the system struggled through summer
  • Clear dryer vents for airflow and fire safety
  • Clean gutters before the first real rain
  • Trim vegetation and clear dry debris for fire prep
  • Walk irrigation for leaks and wasted water
  • Test smoke and CO alarms; replace weak batteries
  • Check weatherstripping as nights cool


Small fixes now usually cost less than emergency work later.


Ask the Expert

Q: Fall leasing is slower and my vacant home has more days on market. Should I drop the rent right away?

Not automatically. Start with current comps, property condition, and showing feedback. If applicants like the home but hesitate on price, a modest adjustment or targeted make-ready (paint, flooring, yard, better photos) often beats sitting empty. If showings are scarce, marketing and presentation may be the first problem, not the rent alone. Long vacancy has a real cost, so a thoughtful small move early often beats holding an ambitious number for months.


Have a question for a future issue? Tell us what you want covered.


����Help Us Become Best Property Management Company 2026

item.content:encoded:
After a summer of turns, heat, and after-hours calls, Redding owners get a quiet week to decide if self-managing is still worth it.

Summer Was Loud. Fall Is When Owners Decide.


Summer in Redding does not stay on the calendar. It lives in your phone.


If you self-manage a rental here, or in Anderson , Shasta Lake , Cottonwood , or anywhere in Shasta County , the last few months probably looked like this. A turn that ran long. An AC call on a 108-degree afternoon. A showing that ate Saturday. A text at 9 p.m. that was not actually an emergency, except you still had to decide.


Labor Day is behind us. The heat is easing. School is in. This is the first quiet stretch a lot of owners get all year. It is also the moment to be honest about whether you still want the landlord hat.


We Make Rentals Simple. For a self-managing owner, simple starts with not being the after-hours desk.


What a hard summer actually costs you


The rent check is not the whole story. The summer bill is time, and it does not show up on a spreadsheet.


  • After-hours calls you triaged in the driveway
  • Vendor hunts when every good tech was already booked
  • Turns that sat empty while you waited on paint, carpet, or a key
  • Showings that collided with work, kids, or a weekend you meant to keep
  • Notices, deposits, and the awkward conversations that never feel like “just five minutes”
  • The low-grade worry that something else will break before you sit down


None of that means you did a bad job. It means the job is a job. California rentals do not run on good intentions. They run on screening, notices, maintenance, and follow-through, including on days you already had plans. A simple test for fall


You do not need a spreadsheet for this. Answer these out loud.


  • Did summer leave you tired of your own rental?
  • Did a repair wait because you were the bottleneck?
  • Did you skip a showing or a notice because you were slammed?
  • Would you hire this job if it were someone elses house?
  • If next summer looks like this one, are you okay with that?


If you said yes to the last one, stay the course. Tighten your vendor list. Put a real after-hours plan on paper. Treat fall like a reset, not a victory lap.


If you hesitated, that is the signal. Fall is when good owners make the change, before the next heat wave, the next school-year move, and the next holiday that lands on their phone.


What changes when the calls are not yours


You still own the house. You still see the invoices. Bigger repairs still get a conversation.

We are local. Not a franchise. Not a call center. We live in this market, and we do this work every day so you do not have to.


Pricing is on the site. No mystery pitch.

Call the office at 530-410-6085 . Tell us what you own and what you want off your plate.


Fall is a clean handoff. Leasing traffic is not the summer rush, which is exactly why this is a good time to get the house, the file, and the resident relationship onto a team that does this for a living.


You can keep self-managing. A lot of owners will. The owners who sleep better are usually the ones who decided the summer was enough data.


Wrap Up


A hard summer is useful. It shows you the real cost of being the manager.


If you still want the work, own that and build a better system. If you do not, let Authority Property Management take the next season so your rental stops running your calendar. Read our Labor Day Should Be Your Last On-Call Holiday guide.

item.title: Mid-Year Investment Check-In: Is Your Rental Portfolio on Track for Q4?
item.description: Real estate investors can use the mid-year mark to plan year-end tax strategies and decide whether refinancing, selling, or expanding fits their goals before Q4.
item.content:encoded:
Four months of runway is all it takes to turn a reactive Q4 into an intentional one.

August is a good time to pause and look at how your rental portfolio has performed so far this year. With four months left before year-end, you still have time to make strategic moves instead of scrambling in December. Here is what to review now so your portfolio heads into Q4 in good shape.

Start With Your Numbers

Before making any big decisions, get a clear picture of where you stand. Pull together:

  • Year-to-date rental income and expenses
  • Occupancy rates across your properties
  • Cash flow per unit
  • Any properties underperforming their projected returns

This gives you a baseline for everything else on this list.

Plan Your Year-End Tax Strategy Now

Waiting until December to think about taxes usually means missed opportunities. Late summer is the right time to talk with your accountant about:

1. Depreciation and cost segregation

If you purchased a property this year, a cost segregation study can accelerate depreciation and increase your deductions. These studies take time to complete, so starting now avoids a year-end rush.

2. Capital gains planning

If you are considering selling a property, know your capital gains exposure ahead of time. This gives you room to explore options like a 1031 exchange before the sale closes.

3. Expense timing

Some repairs, upgrades, or prepaid expenses may be worth completing before December 31 if they support your tax position. Your accountant can help you decide what makes sense this year versus next.

4. Retirement and entity structuring

Mid-year is also a smart time to review whether your current business structure, such as an LLC, still fits your portfolio , and whether contributions to a retirement account tied to your real estate income make sense.

Decide: Refinance, Sell, or Expand?

Once your numbers and tax plan are in place, it is time to look at strategy for each property.

Consider refinancing if:

  • Interest rates have shifted favorably since your original loan
  • You want to pull out equity to fund your next purchase
  • Your current loan terms no longer match your goals

Consider selling if:

  • A property has consistently underperformed despite good management
  • You want to reposition capital into a stronger market or asset type
  • The property no longer fits your long-term strategy

Consider expanding if:

  • Your cash flow supports a down payment on a new property
  • You have identified a market with strong rental demand
  • Your portfolio has capacity for more debt without added risk

There is no single right answer here. The goal is to make an intentional decision based on your numbers, not a reactive one based on market noise.

Set Your Q4 Priorities

With four months left in the year, pick two or three priorities and commit to them. That might mean finalizing a refinance application, listing an underperforming property, or lining up financing for your next acquisition. Whatever you choose, doing it now with a full picture of your portfolio puts you in a much stronger position than waiting until the last quarter to react. A mid-year check-in will not fix every issue on its own, but it gives you the runway to make thoughtful, well-timed decisions before the year closes out.

item.title: August 2026 Redding Rental Market Update
item.description: Redding's August rental market shows steady leasing activity, investor opportunities, tax insights, rent cap updates, and practical tips for owners.
item.content:encoded:
Leasing, Investing & Local Wins

Strong leasing activity, local investment wins, community recognition, and practical insights for Redding rental property owners and investors.

August has given us plenty to talk about. The Redding rental market is moving, local investors are making moves of their own, and our Authority Property Management team has had a busy summer both in and out of the office.


This month, we’re looking at our latest vacancy and leasing numbers, a successful local fourplex transaction, an important California rent cap update, rental property depreciation, and some exciting recognition for our team.


As always, our focus is helping owners, investors, and residents navigate rental housing in Shasta County with less stress.


��️ Redding Rental Market Update

If the last 30 days are any indication, renters are still moving.

Authority Property Management completed 36 move-ins over the past 30 days , while our residential portfolio is currently running at a 6.3% vacancy rate .

That activity tells us this is not a stagnant Redding rental market. Properties are turning over and new residents are moving in. At the same time, renters have choices. Pricing, property condition, marketing, and responsiveness continue to matter. Owners who stay realistic about pricing and keep their properties clean, maintained, and move-in ready are in a much better position to capture current demand.


For Redding rental property owners, this is a good time to pay attention to days on market and showing activity rather than relying only on what a property rented for last year.


�� Shasta County Sales Market Snapshot

The sales side of the market is moving too.


Josh Barker’s most recent Shasta County market report available during our research showed 989 closed sales through May 2026 , compared with 867 during the same period in 2025. That represented a 14.1% increase in year-to-date sales , despite continued pressure from mortgage rates.

We’re seeing some of that investor activity firsthand.

Recently, one Authority PM owner decided to sell a fourplex while another Authority PM owner was looking to buy. The property transferred from one client to another and closed in just 35 days .


It was an incredibly smooth transaction and a great example of something we have noticed lately. Some investors are choosing to move cash into real estate and expand their portfolios when the right opportunity comes along.

Every investment is different, but opportunities like this remind us that real estate investing in Redding is about more than interest rates. Price, rental income, expenses, tax strategy, property condition, and long-term goals all play a role.


�� Investor Corner: Are You Accounting for Depreciation?

Speaking of investment strategy, there is another part of rental property ownership that is easy to overlook: depreciation .

Rental property performance is about more than the difference between rent collected and bills paid each month. Depending on an owner's individual circumstances, depreciation may reduce taxable rental income even while a property is producing positive cash flow. For most residential rental buildings using the federal General Depreciation System, the depreciable building basis is generally recovered over 27.5 years . Land is generally not depreciable.


We recently published a new resource to make this concept easier to understand.

Read it here: https://www.authoritypm.com/rental-property-depreciation-tax-deductions-every-landlord-should-know


�� Try Our Rental Property Depreciation Calculator

Our Rental Property Depreciation Calculator allows owners to enter figures such as purchase price, estimated land value, annual rental income, expenses, and when the property was placed in service. The calculator provides a simplified illustration of estimated depreciable basis, depreciation, and how that deduction could affect taxable rental income.


One of the biggest takeaways is simple:

Positive cash flow and taxable rental income are not necessarily the same number.


That is one reason experienced investors look beyond this month's rent check when evaluating the long-term performance of a rental property.

Our calculator is an educational tool and is not tax advice. Depreciation and tax treatment can become complicated, so owners should review their individual circumstances with a CPA or qualified tax professional. You can find the calculator here.  Depreciation Calculator


⚖️ Legislative Lowdown: AB 1482 Rent Cap Update

There is an important number for California rental property owners to know this month.

The North Valley Property Owners Association reports that the updated CPI figure is 3.6%. This means rent increases taking effect after August 1, 2026 may be capped at 8.6% for properties subject to AB 1482 .


Not every rental property is subject to the same rules or exemptions, so owners should not assume the maximum automatically applies to their property.

Before changing rent, review the property's status, applicable limits, and notice requirements. Owners should review questions about their specific property with their attorney or another trusted professional when needed.


�� A Big Thank You to Our Community!

We want to say a sincere thank you to everyone who nominated Authority Property Management for Best of the North State!

Community recognition means a lot to our entire team.


We were also excited to learn that Authority PM is in the running for Property Management Company of the Year through the North Valley Property Owners Association, or NVPOA . NVPOA is a nonprofit rental housing organization currently serving 12 Northern California counties. The organization provides education, advocacy, rental forms, screening resources, networking, and support for property owners and management professionals.


This nomination is especially exciting for us because Authority Property Management won the NVPOA property management award in 2024 .

Being considered again by an organization made up of people who work directly in the Northern California rental housing industry is something our entire team is proud of.


Thank you to everyone who nominated, supported, and continues to trust us. We truly appreciate it.


�� Team Update: Anniversaries, Birthdays & a Few Golf Balls

We have plenty to celebrate around the office this month!

First, congratulations to Cassey on her one-year anniversary with Authority Property Management! We appreciate everything she has contributed during her first year and are glad to have her as part of our team.


We’re also wishing a very Happy Birthday to Vicky and Lucy! ���� We hope they both have a fantastic birthday and want to thank them for everything they bring to the Authority PM team.


We also recently traded the office for golf clubs and headed over to Redding Aqua Golf for a team outing. We had a blast!

Aqua Golf has made some great improvements to the property, and our experience was fantastic. We always enjoy seeing another local Redding business investing in its facility and creating a fun place for our community.


A big thank you to the Aqua Golf team for taking such good care of us.





��️ Late Summer Property Maintenance Tips

August heat in Redding is no joke. A little preventive maintenance now can protect rental properties, improve resident comfort, and reduce surprise service calls.

A few things worth checking this month:

  • HVAC performance: Check filters and address systems that are struggling during peak heat.
  • Dryer vents: Inspect for lint buildup and proper airflow.
  • Exterior gaps: Seal potential pest entry points.
  • Attic ventilation: Proper ventilation becomes especially important during prolonged heat.
  • Irrigation: Look for leaks, overspray, broken emitters, and unnecessary water use.
  • Fire preparation: Keep dry vegetation, leaves, and combustible debris under control.

Small maintenance items handled today can help prevent much larger expenses tomorrow.


�� Ask the Expert

With investors buying again, should I be looking for another rental property?

Maybe, but start with the numbers rather than the excitement.

Look at realistic rent, operating expenses, insurance, property taxes, expected maintenance, financing, vacancy, and the property's long-term potential. Then talk with your tax professional about considerations such as depreciation.

Our recent fourplex transaction is a great example. One investor was ready to exit, another was ready to acquire, and the right property connected those two goals in a smooth 35-day closing.

The best investment is not simply the property you can buy.

It is the property that makes sense for your strategy.


�� We’re Always Here to Help

Whether you are buying another rental, evaluating a property you already own, preparing for a vacancy, or simply trying to understand the Redding rental market, our team is here to help.


At Authority Property Management, We Make Rentals Simple!

item.title: Rental Property Depreciation: Tax Deductions Every Landlord Should Know
item.description: Unlock one of real estate’s biggest tax benefits. Learn how residential rental property depreciation reduces taxable income while your property appreciates in value.
item.content:encoded:
Rental Property Depreciation: One of the Most Valuable Tax Benefits Available to Landlords


Depreciation can allow a landlord to reduce taxable rental income year after year, even while the rental property itself may be increasing in market value.

That sounds strange at first.

How can a property appreciate in value while the IRS allows you to depreciate it at the same time?

That is one of the reasons rental real estate can be such an attractive long-term investment.

At Authority Property Management, we believe rental property owners should understand not only what their property earns each month, but also the larger financial advantages that can come with owning income-producing real estate.

In this article, we will explain how rental property depreciation works, why it can be so valuable, and why every landlord should be discussing it with a qualified tax professional.


Important: This article is for general educational purposes only. Authority Property Management does not provide tax, accounting, or legal advice. Every owner's situation is different. Always consult your CPA or qualified tax professional regarding your specific circumstances.

�� What Is Rental Property Depreciation?

Depreciation is a federal income tax deduction that allows property owners to recover the cost of certain income-producing property over time.

The IRS recognizes that buildings, appliances, flooring, equipment, and other physical assets have useful lives. Instead of necessarily deducting the entire cost in one year, taxpayers generally recover those costs through depreciation deductions over specified periods.

For most residential rental buildings using the federal General Depreciation System, the building is depreciated over 27.5 years .

That creates an annual tax deduction that may significantly reduce the taxable income generated by the rental property.

And here is the part many new landlords find surprising:

Your property does not have to actually be losing market value for you to claim depreciation.

A rental home could increase substantially in market value while the owner continues taking allowable depreciation deductions.


�� Your Property Can Appreciate While You Depreciate It

This is one of the most interesting characteristics of real estate investing.

Imagine buying a rental property in Redding for $450,000 .

Over the next 10 or 15 years, rents may rise, the neighborhood may improve, inflation may increase replacement costs, and the property's market value may grow.

The property could eventually be worth considerably more than the original purchase price.

From an investment standpoint, the property appreciated .

But for tax purposes, the depreciable portion of the property may still be generating annual depreciation deductions.

Those two things can happen at the same time.

That means a real estate investor can potentially benefit from:

  • Rental income
  • Mortgage principal reduction
  • Long-term property appreciation
  • Depreciation deductions
  • Other legitimate rental property tax deductions

That combination is a major reason investors often view real estate differently from many other types of investments.


�� You Cannot Depreciate the Land

One important distinction is that landlords generally depreciate the building , not the land underneath it.

Land generally cannot be depreciated because it does not wear out or become obsolete in the same way a building does.

That means the purchase price generally needs to be allocated between the value of the land and the value of the improvements.

For example:

Purchase Price: $450,000
Allocated Land Value: $90,000
Building Basis: $360,000

The $90,000 attributed to land would generally not be depreciated.

The $360,000 building basis generally would be.

Using a simplified 27.5-year calculation:

$360,000 ÷ 27.5 = approximately $13,091 per year in depreciation

The actual first and final year calculations will generally differ because residential rental property uses the mid-month convention. This example is intentionally simplified to demonstrate the concept.

Think about what that means.

The landlord did not necessarily write a $13,091 check that year.

Yet there may still be approximately $13,091 of depreciation expense reducing taxable rental income before considering the owner's other tax circumstances and limitations.

That is why depreciation is commonly described as a non-cash deduction .


�� Why Depreciation Can Be So Valuable

Imagine that same rental property produces positive cash flow.

After collecting rent and paying operating expenses, the owner has $12,000 remaining for the year before depreciation .

Now assume the property also generates approximately $13,091 of depreciation .

From a cash standpoint, the owner may have received positive cash flow.

From a tax accounting standpoint, depreciation could significantly reduce the taxable income associated with the property and, depending on the owner's circumstances, could potentially contribute to a tax loss.

That does not automatically mean the landlord can deduct the entire loss against wages or other income.

Rental real estate can be subject to passive activity rules, at-risk rules, and other limitations.

But this example demonstrates why experienced real estate investors pay close attention to depreciation.

�� Tip: Positive cash flow and taxable income are not necessarily the same number.

�� When Does Rental Property Depreciation Start?

Buying a rental property does not necessarily mean depreciation begins on the closing date.

Generally, depreciation begins when the property is placed in service for the production of income .

In practical terms, this usually means the property is ready and available to rent.

For example, imagine you purchase a home in May but spend June and July completing renovations.

If the property becomes rent-ready and is offered for rent in August, August may be the relevant placed-in-service month rather than May.

That distinction can matter when calculating the first year's depreciation.

Good documentation is important.

Rental property owners should retain records such as:

  • Closing statements
  • Purchase documents
  • Improvement invoices
  • Contractor receipts
  • Appliance receipts
  • Renovation records
  • Dates the property became available for rent
  • Documents supporting the property's tax basis

�� Repairs and Improvements Are Not Always Treated the Same

Another important tax concept for landlords is the difference between a repair and an improvement .

Repair costs may sometimes be currently deductible when they keep the property in ordinarily efficient operating condition.

Improvements may need to be capitalized and depreciated over time.

For example, replacing a small damaged component may receive different tax treatment from replacing an entire major building system.

A new roof, for example, is generally treated differently from a small roof repair.

This is one reason good bookkeeping matters so much for rental property owners.

Simply labeling everything as "maintenance" does not determine how the IRS will treat the expense.

Your CPA needs enough information to understand what work was actually completed.


��️ Some Rental Property Assets Depreciate Much Faster

The rental building itself may generally have a 27.5-year recovery period , but not every asset associated with a rental property necessarily has the same depreciation schedule.

Certain assets commonly found in residential rentals may have shorter recovery periods.

Depending on the circumstances, these may include items such as:

  • Appliances
  • Carpeting
  • Certain furniture
  • Equipment
  • Certain land improvements
  • Other qualifying property components

This becomes particularly important when an owner makes substantial improvements or purchases a larger investment property.

Instead of assuming every dollar associated with the property must be depreciated over 27.5 years, a qualified tax professional may identify assets that receive different tax treatment.


That leads to a strategy many real estate investors are hearing much more about.


�� What Is Cost Segregation?

A cost segregation study analyzes components of a building to determine whether certain costs can properly be classified into shorter depreciation categories rather than remaining part of the building's longer depreciation schedule.

Depending on the property, certain components may potentially be assigned to 5-year, 7-year, 15-year, or other appropriate recovery periods.

The goal is not to create deductions that do not exist.

The goal is to determine when legitimate depreciation deductions may be taken .

Moving qualifying assets into shorter recovery periods can accelerate depreciation deductions into earlier years.

That can potentially improve an investor's current cash flow by reducing current tax liabilities, depending on the owner's individual tax situation.

Cost segregation is not appropriate for every rental property.

Factors that should be considered include:

  • Property value
  • Depreciable basis
  • Cost of the study
  • Planned holding period
  • Passive activity limitations
  • Other income
  • Future tax planning
  • The owner's overall financial situation

A qualified CPA or cost segregation professional should help determine whether the strategy makes financial sense.


⚡ Bonus Depreciation Can Make This Even More Interesting

Current federal tax law also provides 100% additional first-year depreciation , commonly called bonus depreciation, for certain qualifying property acquired after January 19, 2025, assuming applicable requirements are met.

This does not mean a landlord can simply deduct the entire cost of a residential rental building in the first year.

Residential rental buildings generally remain 27.5-year property.

However, certain qualifying shorter-life assets associated with a rental property may potentially qualify for bonus depreciation.

That makes conversations about asset classification and cost segregation particularly important for investors purchasing or substantially improving rental property.

�� Pro Tip: Before making a major rental property purchase or renovation, consider talking with your CPA before the transaction is complete instead of waiting until tax season.

Tax planning can give your professional more opportunities to structure and document transactions correctly before the money has already been spent.


�� California Landlords Need to Be Especially Careful

California rental property owners have another layer to consider.

California depreciation rules do not always match federal depreciation rules.

Federal tax law and California tax law may treat certain depreciation deductions differently, including some forms of bonus depreciation.

That means a California rental property owner could potentially have one depreciation calculation for federal tax purposes and another calculation for California tax purposes.

For Redding and Shasta County rental property owners, this distinction is especially important.

Do not assume that a federal tax strategy automatically produces the exact same California tax result.

Your CPA may need to maintain separate federal and California depreciation schedules.


�� What Happens if Depreciation Creates a Rental Loss?

This is where depreciation becomes powerful, but also more complicated.

Rental activities are generally treated as passive activities for federal income tax purposes unless an exception applies.

Passive losses can be subject to limitations.

Some landlords who actively participate in their rental real estate may qualify for a special allowance that permits up to $25,000 of rental real estate losses to offset certain nonpassive income.

However, that allowance is subject to income limits and other requirements.

Different rules can also apply to taxpayers who qualify as real estate professionals and meet applicable material participation requirements.

Losses that cannot currently be used may potentially be suspended and carried forward rather than simply disappearing.

This is why a statement such as:

"Depreciation will automatically reduce the taxes on your W-2 income."

is an oversimplification.

Sometimes depreciation-related losses may offset other income.

Sometimes they may not.

Sometimes the tax benefit may be carried forward.

The answer depends on the taxpayer's individual situation.


⚠️ What About Depreciation Recapture When You Sell?

Depreciation provides a valuable tax benefit during property ownership, but landlords also need to understand what can happen when the property is eventually sold.

Depreciation reduces the property's adjusted tax basis.

When depreciated real estate is sold for a gain, some of the gain associated with depreciation may receive different tax treatment.

This concept is commonly referred to as depreciation recapture , although the exact tax treatment of real estate depreciation can be more technical than the phrase suggests.

This sometimes leads owners to ask:

"Should I just skip depreciation so I don't have to deal with it when I sell?"

Generally, that is not a good assumption.

Tax basis is generally reduced by depreciation that was allowed or allowable .

In other words, simply failing to claim depreciation may not allow an owner to avoid the tax consequences associated with depreciation they were entitled to take.

That is an important conversation to have with your CPA.

The rules surrounding a future sale, suspended passive losses, capital gains, depreciation, Section 1250 gain, and other planning strategies can become complicated.

The lesson is not that depreciation is bad because taxes may eventually be due.

The lesson is that good real estate investing includes planning for the entire ownership cycle, from purchase through eventual sale.


�� Depreciation Shows the Difference Between Cash Flow and Taxable Income

This may be the biggest concept rental property owners should understand.

A rental property has several different measurements of financial performance.

There is:

  • Cash flow
  • Taxable income
  • Equity growth
  • Mortgage principal reduction
  • Property appreciation
  • Operating expenses
  • Tax deductions
  • Depreciation

These numbers interact, but they are not identical.

A rental property can generate positive cash flow while showing much less taxable income because of depreciation.

A property can appreciate in market value while its tax basis is being reduced through depreciation.

A landlord can also increase equity by paying down a mortgage even though mortgage principal payments are generally not treated as a deductible operating expense.

Understanding those differences helps property owners evaluate rental real estate as a long-term investment instead of simply looking at the rent check that arrives each month.


�� Good Records Make Good Tax Planning Possible

A CPA can only work with the information an owner provides.


Rental property owners should maintain organized records for:

  • Property purchases
  • Closing costs
  • Improvements
  • Repairs
  • Appliances
  • Flooring
  • Roof replacements
  • HVAC systems
  • Capital projects
  • Contractor work
  • Major property upgrades
  • Other significant expenditures


Keep documentation showing:

  • What was purchased
  • What work was completed
  • When it was completed
  • How much it cost
  • When the asset or improvement was placed in service


That information may help determine whether an expense is currently deductible, depreciable over several years, assigned to a shorter recovery period, or potentially eligible for another tax treatment.

Poor records can turn legitimate tax opportunities into missed deductions.
